We agree with the Director's determination that the above-referenced documentation does not
establish that the PEET award is a nationally or internationally recognized award for excellence in the
field. The Petitioner relies on letters and material from the issuing entity and its parent organization.
The Petitioner did not submit evidence of the national or international recognition of the Beneficiary's
particular PEET award, such as national or widespread local coverage of her award in science or general
media. The plain language of this criterion specifically requires that the Beneficiary's award be nationally
or internationally recognized in the field of endeavor and it is the Petitioner's burden to establish every
element of this criterion. The record does not contain documentary evidence showing that the
Beneficiary's specific PEET award has garnered recognition beyond the presenting organization and
is therefore commensurate with a nationally or internationally recognized prize or award for excellence
in the field.
In light of the above, the Petitioner did not demonstrate that the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion.

Documentation of the alien's membership in associations in the field for which
class[fication is sought, which require outstanding achievements of their members as
judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or _fields.
8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2).
3
In order to demonstrate that membership in an association meets this criterion, a petitioner must show
that the association requires outstanding achievement as an essential condition for admission to
membership. Membership requirements based on employment or activity in a given field, minimum
education or experience, recommendations by colleagues or current members, or payment of dues, do
not satisfy this criterion as such requirements do not constitute outstanding achievements. Further,
the overall prestige of a given association is not determinative; the issue here is membership
requirements rather than the association's overall reputation.

consideration the established criteria on Art 8 of the By-laws. Professional-level, Curriculum Vitae
and academic support. Prestige within the Society: Merit and recognition for the candidate
performance in the field related with the Objectives of the Society." We note that the record lacks
the entity's bylaws, or other official documents, detailing its membership criteria. Regardless,
eligibility criteria based on such educational and professional requirements as "Professional-level,
Curriculum Vitae and academic support" and "Merit and recognition for the candidate's performance
in the field" do not satisfy this criterion as such requirements do not constitute "outstanding
achievements" in the field.
Based on the above reasons, the Petitioner has not satisfied this criterion.

In light of the foregoing, we agree with the Director's determination that the Petitioner has not satisfied
the requirements of this regulatory criterion.

releases and certificates pertaining to the !municipal recycling program. While it appears that
the Beneficiary's organization designed this program, the evidence does not establish that the program
was an original contribution of major significance in the field.
In order to satisfy this criterion, the petitioner must establish not only that the beneficiary has made
original contributions but that they have been of major significance in the field. For example, it may
support the record with evidence that a beneficiary's contributions have been widely implemented,
have remarkably impacted or influenced the field, or have otherwise risen to a level of major
significance in the field. Demonstrating ability as a skilled geographer in the field of environmental
management and sustainability is not itself a contribution of major significance; rather, the Petitioner
must demonstrate that the Beneficiary has impacted the field as a whole. Cf Visinscaia v. Beers, 4 F.
Supp. 3d 126, 134-135 (D.D.C. 2013) (upholding a finding that a ballroom dancer had not met a similar
criterion in the regulations pertaining to immigrants of extraordinary ability because she did not
demonstrate her impact in the field as a whole).
The record does not include documentary evidence showing the widespread implementation of the
Beneficiary's work, that it has been seminal, or that it otherwise equates to an original contribution of
major significance in the field. USCIS may, in its discretion, use as advisory opinions statements
submitted as expert testimony. See Matter o_f Caron International, 19 I&N Dec. 791, 795 (Comm'r
1988). However, USCIS is ultimately responsible for making the final determination regarding an
individual's eligibility for the benefit sought. Id. Here, the preceding letters of recommendation
demonstrate that the Beneficiary is admired for her skills in the field of environmental management
and sustainability, and that her work on projects has benefited her clients and earned the respect and
